content: Large for gestational age (LGA) refers to infants whose birth weight exceeds the 90th percentile for their gestational age. The term macrosomia, also known as big baby syndrome, is sometimes used interchangeably with LGA. However, macrosomia can also be specifically defined as a fetus weighing more than 4000 grams (8 pounds 13 ounces) or 4500 grams (9 pounds 15 ounces), regardless of gestational age. LGA is typically diagnosed after birth, as fetal size and weight are not routinely measured during the later stages of pregnancy. However, some LGA fetuses may be identified during routine ultrasounds, although late-pregnancy fetal weight estimations are often imprecise. There is also a suspected association between LGA and polyhydramnios, a condition characterized by excessive amniotic fluid. One of the primary risk factors for LGA is poorly controlled diabetes, particularly gestational diabetes (GD) or preexisting diabetes mellitus (DM). Elevated maternal plasma glucose and insulin levels can stimulate excessive fetal growth. LGA newborns exposed to maternal diabetes often exhibit increased weight without proportional increases in other measurements. In contrast, LGA infants without maternal diabetes exposure typically have universal measurements above the 90th percentile. Additional factors that may predispose to LGA include: Prolonged pregnancies beyond 40 weeks, which increase the likelihood of LGA. Male infants, who tend to weigh more than female infants. Genetic factors, as taller and heavier parents are more likely to have larger babies. Maternal obesity significantly raises the risk. Excessive maternal weight gain during pregnancy. Multiparity, as mothers with multiple previous pregnancies are 2-3 times more likely to have LGA infants compared to first-time mothers. Congenital anomalies, such as transposition of the great vessels. Erythroblastosis fetalis, a condition involving severe fetal anemia. The use of certain antibiotics during pregnancy, such as amoxicillin or pivampicillin. Ethnic background, with LGA being more common in mothers of African origin, partly due to the higher prevalence of diabetes in this population. The delivery of an LGA infant can present challenges, particularly if the baby's head size is disproportionate to the mother's pelvic diameter. Vaginal delivery may become complicated, with shoulder dystocia being one of the most common complications. To ensure the safety of both mother and baby, cesarean sections are often performed in such cases to avoid birth canal lacerations and other complications. After birth, early feeding is critical to prevent neonatal hypoglycemia, a common issue in LGA infants. Prompt identification and management of any individual complications are essential for optimal outcomes.
